utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Sorry about the delayed start. Apparently the previous hearing ran over in time a little. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start, Your Honours, there are three corrections to be made to the transcript material. Corrections, so may I be permitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Since LiveNote has not yet been updated to the Word form, what I have is the LiveNote pages, not transcript page numbers. I'm referring to page 38 of LiveNote, line 10. The witness indicated that the position which he marked as "B" on the map came into existence in the second half of December. However, it has gone down on the record as the second half of November, so it should be corrected to read as "second half of December."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then the next correction is at page 50, line 22. I asked a question with regard to the park named Gradac, and indicated it as which is below Bogisica Park, but it has -- the record has gone down as Bosanka. So the word "Bosanka" to be read as Bogisica Park.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The third correction is at page 65, line 13. The witness marked the Maljutka at Hotel President in Lapad in the second mark with the marking letter "D," but the record does down as "B." So the record to be corrected as "D."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I just remind you, Mr. Negodic, of the affirmation you took at the beginning, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Negodic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At close of sessions last evening, we were discussing the anti-aircraft position which is indicated to the north of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown the map we were discussing yesterday. Both maps, perhaps. That is, map bearing P159, and the second one which he was marking.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When I asked you, Mr. Negodic, as to if you were aware as to if the anti-aircraft position indicated to the north of the Old Town was at that location on 6th December 1991, you indicated a degree of uncertainty and went on to say that there was an alternative position at the Gradac Park for that particular weapon. And you indicated the park which is depicted to the west of the Old Town, on the coastal line. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could place -- I think the map which is on the ELMO is the wrong map. The wrong one. It should be the other map that should be on the ELMO. So could you please -- yes, you're placing the pointer at the position. Now, could you indicate as to of these two positions, which position was considered as the basic combat position for that weapon and which was considered as the reserve position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you indicate as to what criteria is used to determine as to which position should be used as the basic combat position and which as the reserve? I'm not referring to these particular positions. Generally, what is the criteria used?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At our meetings, we decided which the main axis of attack the enemy would take, and that's where we set up our basic combat positions. This tentative attack, should the enemy attack from another direction, then there must be an alternative combat position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Considering the nature of the attack on 6 December, what would you have considered to be the most suitable position out of these two positions to place the weapon?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as anti-aircraft defence is concerned, I'm not a professional in that sphere myself, but I think that I am sufficiently trained, generally speaking, for me to conclude that a better combat position would be this one here, the one I'm indicating on the map now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is the position at Gradac Park?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you explain the reasons behind your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, air attacks that took place in November 1991, when the Srdj fort was targeted, I think that a better place for targeting was from that hill rather than in the depression between the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you explain as to what that position, the north of the Old Town, looks like, and what is it? Are there houses there, structures? What exactly is that place?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were located at the cable-car, the lower part, which goes up to Fort Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And from there, what are the positions one could target with an anti-aircraft weapon?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, these two positions, the ones we're discussing at the cable-car and to the east of that, was intended for aircrafts alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And on 6 December 1991, were there any attacks carried out by aircrafts?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In that context, what would anti-aircraft weapons be used where there are no aircraft attacks carried out? Do you use for alternative targets?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You indicated earlier on with regard to the two previous anti-aircraft positions, especially the first one we discussed about, that you recall seeing that particular position firing on the 6th of December, 1991, because you remember seeing the third round, which was a tracer. That was -- that being an aircraft -- anti-aircraft weapon --

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I said was that -- was this: In the Orshan area, I saw a three-barrel weapon, because every fourth or fifth bullet is a tracer bullet. That's what I said. The one we are talking about was Strela, that position. The Strela 2-M was there, and the so-called Igla, or pin weapon, and that is intended exclusively for aircrafts and was not used on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So is it the position that a three-barrelled anti-aircraft weapon can be used on positions other than aircrafts, on alternative targets as opposed to the anti-aircraft weapon referred to as Strela?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And as I've already said, this three-barrelled weapon targeted the peak and surrounding areas of Srdj and Fort Srdj as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can a single-barrelled or double-barrelled anti-aircraft be used to target positions other than aircrafts? I'm sorry, "anti-aircraft weapon," it should read.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The infantry and some lighter targets. But in 99 per cent of the cases, it is only for the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And your position is that a Strela -- or, I'm sorry, my pronunciation might be bad, but Igla, or pin weapon, cannot be used on anything, against any other target other than an aircraft? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say it cannot, but it would be too costly a device to deploy for any other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea about the cost of a single projectile used for a Strela or an Igla weapon?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is it relatively more expensive than other forms of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Many times over.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, according to what you said, the position indicated north of the Old Town, if in fact it was deployed on the 6th of December, would have had either a Strela or an Igla weapon.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can't call that a position per se, as such. It's a device that you place on your shoulder. It takes three minutes to put it into a small vehicle and transfer it to another position if we can call it a position at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been informed that there is a transcript error. May I just take a moment to find that out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I will check this during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Negodic, for that interruption.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, initially when I asked you as to whether your forces had anti-aircraft weapons, you indicated four weapons; a three-barrelled weapon, a single- or double-barrelled weapon, a Strela, and an Igla. Now, so far we have gone through this map with regard to three positions, containing three of those weapons. Would you please drag your pointer down to the balance position, the fourth anti-aircraft position. It's to the east of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Negodic. I'm talking about the fourth position we did not deal with so far. That is to the east of the Old Town. You just pointed the position we've already dealt with.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you indicate as to what is that location known as?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: We call that Ploce, or Zlatni Potok.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what was the weapon? Obviously it's an anti-aircraft weapon. Do you know what was positioned there? Was it the Strela or the Igla? Because that's --

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. It could have either been -- it could have been one or the other at any of these two places, either the Strela or the Igla.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So between the two positions, the position indicated north of the Old Town and the east of the Old Town, it could have been either the Strela or the Igla?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And both these weapons you indicated were generally used only against aircrafts?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know if the position at -- towards the east of the Old Town fired on 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say "no," is it the case of you don't know, or is it that it did not fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not fire, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that the first -- at the first position, the anti-aircraft weapon which was there was on a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was on a truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The second position, was it on a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that second position. I don't know any of the details there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The Strela and the Igla, how were they used? Were they mobile? Were they used from vehicles, or were they fixed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have fixed positions. They would be transported on vehicles, according to need.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know if any of those -- any -- I'm sorry. Let me rephrase that. Do you know the anti-aircraft weapon which was mounted on a vehicle, which is the first question, was ever used within the walls of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it ever present within the Old Town? And I'm giving the time period 1st October 1991 to 31st December 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single anti-aircraft weapon of the artillery or anything else entered the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Apart from the four positions indicated here with regard to the anti-aircraft weapons' position, do you know if there were any other anti-aircraft positions existing on the 6th of December, 1991 which are not depicted on this map?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, there were no other positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you made two amendments -- not two. You made four amendments to this map. You drew squares around two positions which were not there on the 6th of December, 1991, being the mortar position at the position marked "B" and the ZIS cannon position at the position marked -- I beg your pardon, Your Honours. I need to get the markings right. Position marked "C." It was ZIS cannon.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Montovjerna combat position, if I might be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And then you added two positions to the map being positions that were there on the 6th of December, 1991, which are not reflected in this map, being the Maljutka position at Hotel President in Lapad, by the coastal line, the position marked "D"; and the position at Mala Petka, which is the position marked "C."

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, subject to these amendments, sir, would you say the second map now reflects all mortars, artillery, and aircraft weapons which were in place on the 6th of December, 1991? Subject to those four amendments.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Therefore, in reference to mortars positions and artillery positions, anti-aircraft weapon positions, does this second map now reflect the ground situation as at 6 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are there -- do you know -- I beg your pardon. Let me rephrase it. Were there any positions on the 6th of December, 1991 in place which are now not reflected on these two maps?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is there any artillery, mortar, or anti-aircraft positions indicated on these two maps, and subject to the amendments, which were not there on the 6th of December, 1991? And I'm saying subject to the amendments. With the exception of those two -- those positions that you drew squares around which you said were not there on the 6th of December, 1991. With the exception of those, are there any that are indicated here which were not there on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say "that's right," sir, you mean the positions now reflected there are all as at 6 December 1991, with the exception of those which are indicated with squares?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The positions that we drew on the map, the positions that we later corrected, that's the situation on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I don't intend to take too much of time with regard to the other markings on this second map, Mr. Negodic, but for purpose of information: Would you briefly indicate as to what the orange lines and the blue lines, the broken lines on the map, depict. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: These red lines are used to mark positions of some of our forces, and the blue lines are used to mark enemy positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say "positions," are you talking about infantry positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And could you give us some idea as to about how many soldiers are deployed at a given line, one of those broken lines. And I'm talking about the red lines, your positions.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with details. There was simply no time for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you be able to give us an approximate idea, approximately how many soldiers were deployed at a given position? Not every position, but --

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: This red line here, each of these red lines may be used to mark positions occupied by 1 person or by 11 persons. So that's only generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you give some indication as to about how many soldiers were deployed around the wider city of Dubrovnik, in the infantry positions. And I'm talking about on your side.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, towards the fort of Srdj, between 120 and 140 men. As for the infantry, I can only generalise, because there's no way I can know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea as to what those black boxes with the circles there indicate? What do they depict? There is a line of black boxes just in front of your confrontation line. What do they indicate?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: They indicate minefields on the slopes of Srdj, just above the road. The road running along the upper side of the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of those positions? Was it to prevent the onslaught of enemy troops?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was used to prevent infantry attacks against Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And could you give us a general idea as to what the rectangular objects within your lines are, that is, the ones indicated with black and white, as well as the black circles.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to your first question, that's how we marked shelters. Some sort of a field shelter. As for the black circles, the circles that are drawn along the access roads, those were probably surprise mines or something along these lines. If I may just add a commentary to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: These questions should be addressed to a professional soldier. I am no professional soldier myself. I'm just trying to help clarify the situation that prevailed on the 6th of December and prior to that date. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what I was trying to do, Mr. Negodic, and we will not pursue this map any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I move to tender this map in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked P160.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, in the course of an operation, who decides as to which of your artillery or mortar positions should fire, and at which targets? Who decides that? As chief of artillery, is it your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main order would have been given by the defence commander, Nojko Marinovic. In the course of combat operations, I, Ivan Negodic, would be the one to give the orders. I can add a clarification. The reason that I was the one who gave the orders was because that was my position. I was the commander, the chief of artillery, and an observer. I was the chief of reconnaissance unit. Therefore, I had a twofold capacity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: As such, sir, is it correct to say that you would have been thus in a position to know exactly which of your positions fired at which targets on 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, naturally, I would have been in a position. I had to be familiar with this, because that was the only way to guide our own fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And would that be the case even with regard to operations conducted in -- or perhaps let me rephrase it. Your responses to JNA operations conducted in October and November 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: With regard to your fire missions conducted in October, and I'm referring to the time period 23rd, 24th October, and fire missions conducted in November, and I'm referring to the period 8 November to 13th November, would it have been during this period also you who would have decided as to which Croatian positions fired at which JNA targets?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where were you on 6 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at combat position occupied by 76 millimetres ZIS cannon near the bridge, on Ivo Vojnovic Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You responded to one of my questions that the crew at the position near the SDK building, which is the crew commanded by Primic, was at that particular position on 6 December 1991. Now, how do you know this, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because I was the one who gave the order. I'll explain, if I may, why the order was given to begin with. That unit was at two different combat positions. One was near the SDK building, and the other was at about 120 metres to the east of the Old Town. The purpose of this other position was to prevent infantry attacks from the east, which means from the Dubac area. As the engineering unit had laid mines along that direction and, and as there was firing from all kinds of weapons, accompanied by an infantry attack and tanks, the meaning of that particular combat position was lost. An order was given to evacuate the people, to withdraw the people, and not to open fire from there, because it was too near the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you at any stage during the 6th of December, 1991, visit the position near SDK building?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At about 11.30, I was informed that we had run out of ammunition. They said I should do something in order to improve the situation. I got into my car and drove over to the combat positions. I couldn't find the commander or the deputy commander. They had left for another combat position at Lazaret, because there were four mines there that they had gone there to fetch.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At that time you visited the particular position, was the entire crew there, with the exception of the commander and the deputy?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found the entire crew there in the basement of the SDK building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 6th of December, 1991, were you in a position to observe the Croat fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except from the mortar positions, which was at Solitudo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: During the period 1st October 1991 to 31st December 1991, did you at any stage have a mortar or an artillery piece mounted on a vehicle, a truck or pick-up?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did use a small car with a small trailer to transfer a Maljutka from its initial combat position to alternative combat positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Apart from using a vehicle to transport weapons, did you use any of your heavy weapons on a vehicle from particular positions to fire at JNA as means of provocation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have to provide two answers to this question. Such weapons cannot be mounted on a vehicle, to begin with. And secondly, as for our part, I guarantee there were no provocations. There is not a single country on this planet where you find defenders carrying out acts of provocation. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps explain your response when you said "such weapons cannot be mounted on a vehicle." Why not? Can you give the reasons therefor?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ZIS gun and the mortars require a hard surface for a platform. The guns, and in the case of mortars, it needs to be something softer, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. like the ground, to absorb the shock of firing. So that is one reason why it cannot be mounted on a truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What you're saying is a truck or a vehicle would not have the appropriate surface to fire a mortar from, due to the fact that it would not have sufficient soft surface to absorb the recoil that you get when you fire such a weapon?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How about a recoilless cannon, for instance, which does not require a soft surface? Could you not use a vehicle for such a weapon?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen anything like that so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you used a trailer to transport the Maljutka from one place to the other. At any point, was this trailer parked within the Old Town with the Maljutka in it for some period of time, within the period 1st October 1991 to 31st December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already stated, the initial combat position for the Maljutka was near the Libertas Hotel at Lapad. Its alternative combat position was at the Ploce Gate, to the east of the Old Town. There was no need for that Maljutka to enter the Old Town at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, could you please let us have an idea as to what kind of -- type of weapons were available to your forces positioned at Srdj. Did they have mortars, artillery, or any other type of heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same applies to that as to the Old Town. The fort of Srdj was built by Napoleon Bonaparte, built of stone. The same applies to mortars, the same explanation that I provided in relation to trucks. The defenders at Srdj were carrying small arms, personal weapons, light machine-guns, and a hand-held launcher as an anti-armour weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you say same explanation applies, what you're indicating is that the ground in the fortress was not suitable for placement of mortars and artillery; is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The fort is built of stone, and there is no way you can place a mortar there, and that is the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you not have placed a mortar outside the fort, fortress, on softer ground?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The enemy was so close that this would have been simply suicidal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, who controlled the fortress at Srdj, and can you give your response within the time -- relevant time frames. Now, I know at some stage the Croatian forces controlled Srdj, but can you give the relevant time frames.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the command controlled that point of resistance. I'm referring to Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. My question to you is: When did the Croat forces control the fortress at Srdj? When did they take over that position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately in October, as early as October, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: 6 December 1991 --

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, in relation to your first question, when the JNA attack began, when they landed at Zupa, Dubrovacka and at Kupari, using the support of paramilitary units from Trebinje, our forces had withdrawn to the Bosanka area and then immediately afterwards to the Srdj fortress area. And they stayed there since.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And I take it when you say "since," till 6 December 1991 and afterwards? Yes or no would suffice, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Since the 23rd of October --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. My --

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by the 6th? Yes. Even after the 6th of December, in 1992 and 1993, they were still at Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. And who controlled Zarkovica, and could you give in the context of the relevant time frames.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the withdrawal, Zarkovica had been an abandoned lookout point, Belvedere. After the Croatian forces had withdrawn in the direction of Dubrovnik and the fortress of Srdj, an observation post, a JNA observation post was set up there. This was an observation post and three combat positions; one recoilless gun, one Maljutka, and sometimes a tank also.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when did the JNA set up this post at Zarkovica? Can you give the time frame?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 25th of October, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who controlled Bosanka? Can you respond in the context of the relevant time frames.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the 22nd and the 23rd, or between the 23rd and the 24th, one day it was controlled by the Croatian army, and after that by the JNA and their paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know when the JNA took control of Bosanka? Do you remember the time frame?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty-four hours after Zarkovica was taken, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who controlled the fortress at Strincjera, and the time frame?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian army controlled Strincjera. As I said, during the withdrawal from Zarkovica and Bosanka, at the same time, there was a withdrawal from Strincjera.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And after the withdrawal, did the JNA take over the fortress at Strincjera?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 6th of December, one of the axes of attack on Srdj was through Strincjera. It was a combined infantry and tank armour attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you remember when the JNA took over Strincjera? An approximate time would do, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a while ago the 24th or the 25th. Therefore, it was at about that time. When Bosanka fell, Strincjera fell too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you give us some --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand which month we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The witness made it clear earlier on it was October 23rd, 24th, but I'll ask it again if it's necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was clear to me. I think you can take it that's the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, could you give us some idea as to what the -- can you describe the view from Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Zarkovica, you can see part of Ploce, to the east of Dubrovnik, the Old Town; the Old Town; half the peninsula of Lapad, facing the open sea, half the peninsula. That's as much as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is there a direct line of vision from Zarkovica into the entire Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, now, we discussed about weapons as to the existence of weapons within the Old Town. Could you tell me: Were there any weapons positioned in the Old Town within the period 1st October 1991 to 31st December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already stated, there were no artillery or anti-aircraft weapons in the town itself. There may have been a hunting rifle or the odd pistol.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were there any type of military installation in the Old Town? And I'm talking about perhaps ammunition depots or command post or shelters, military shelters.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No depots, no military facilities at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How about troop movement? Was there any type of troop movement, noticeable troop movement within the Old Town, or concentration of soldiers within the Old Town at any given time within the period 1st October 1991 to 31st December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inhabitants of Dubrovnik were well aware of the fact that soldiers were banned from grouping even near let alone inside the Old Town. That means there was no movement of troops inside the Old Town whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said that soldiers were banned from grouping even near the Old Town. Could you in that context say as to what orders had you and your sector perhaps received prohibiting the placing of weapons in the Old Town or congregating near the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for manpower, you referred to troops. Of course, a gun is operated by soldiers; however, this particular army had not been set up properly by that time. 95 per cent of those soldiers were still wearing civilian clothes. Secondly, as for the artillery, it wasn't only banned for security reasons. Rather, and this will require a lengthy explanation, there are three basic reasons for that. As I've already said, there is no way you could possibly mount a mortar on a truck or Napoleon's Srdj fortress, or a ZIS gun inside the Old Town, because the entire Old Town is made of stone. Secondly, the streets in the Old Town are very narrow, and had it even been possible to place something there, it would have caused more damage to the surrounding houses than to the enemy. Thirdly, you could only point the guns at the sky if you decided to fire from Dubrovnik. There is no way to target anything else but perhaps the sky. There is no way you can place a gun there. There is no way to introduce a gun or a mortar into the Old Town, especially we were banned, as I said, for security reasons to use any weapons from inside, in order to avoid the Old Town being targeted. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of the protected status of the Old Town, the UNESCO status of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was aware of that, as were the European monitors, who, from the Argentina Hotel were able to see the whole of the Old Town before them, and on several occasions they went out with professionals from the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments and made up 40 or 45 reports relating to the damages done to buildings of great historical importance. Now, we really did sincerely hope that not a single mine or shell would target the Old Town, because we thought that the other side too would value its worth. However, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, previously you said that 95 per cent of those soldiers were still wearing civilian clothes. Did that mean that they had the freedom to roam around in the Old Town with their weapons, or -- I did not get your response too clearly. Could you elaborate?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult for us to even come by the weapons and ammunition that we ultimately got. That was our priority. But we weren't given personal weapons and uniforms along with that. That was left for a later stage, better times.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Notwithstanding if you had uniforms or not, were the personnel attached to your forces banned from congregating or moving around within the Old Town, by your command?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each and every commander had received orders from the commander of the town's defence to convey down the line to their subordinates to obey that, and that was done, and it was controlled. We did not wish to give reason, whatever -- any reason at all for shells to target the Old Town at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, can you please indicate what the effect is when you fire a mortar or an artillery from -- on a hard surface. Can you please give us some idea as to what the effect is. What happens to the weapon, or what happens to those who operate the weapon?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might run the risk of making a caricature, but it would be a salto mortale, a death leap from the operator of such an artillery piece, and they might be killed as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is, if I could please -- correct me if I'm wrong -- what you mean is when you fire a mortar or an artillery piece on a hard surface, because there is no soft surface to absorb the recoil, the gun jumps up, isn't that what happens, and injures the operator?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. But I've already said that. And that was true for Srdj and for the town and for the truck. And let me add once more that in the Old Town, between the houses, among the houses, there was more damage done from the explosion, the detonation, rather than from an enemy shell. So it spreads upwards and sideways, so that the damage would be greater after several shells or mines were targeted rather than an enemy mortar that might hit the roof of a house, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you just said that: "And let me add once more that in the Old Town, between the houses, among the houses, there was more damage done from the explosion, the detonation rather than from an enemy shell." Did you mean to say there was or that there would be if a mortar or an artillery piece was fired from within the Old Town? Is that what you meant? There was or there would be?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be. There would be greater damage had that occurred. A detonation would cause greater damage than an enemy mine. That's what I said. I did not say that there was, but that there would be greater damage. In response to your question had we possibly brought in a mortar into the Old Town, I explained to you and gave the explanation that that would have no effect, and even if we were able to mount them on some sand bags, that the damage done would be greater.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the entire surface of the ground of -- within the Old Town, is it made of rock, hard surface?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. One wouldn't want to change the aspects of the Old Town, and we were criticised for not having enough greenery, but we want to preserve it the way it always was, in its original state. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the context of the topography around the Old Town and the height of the structures within the Old Town, was it possible to fire out from within the Old Town with heavy weapons without taking the risk of the projectiles impacting on its own structures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought that had been adequately answered earlier, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I was under the impression he was addressing the hard surface aspect, but if Your Honour feels there's been adequate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think some time ago the witness gave three reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very good, Your Honour. I will withdraw that question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Negodic, did you personally visit the Old Town during the period 1st October 1991 to 31st December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went in the evening on the 6th of December, with some soldiers, to help put out the fires, because several houses were burning. I went in with a squad when there was the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At any stage during the period 1st October 1991 to 31st December 1991, were there any mortars or artillery pieces positioned or firing from the top of the fortresses of the Old Town? And when I say "fortresses," I'm referring to the four turrets around the walls.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. Only perhaps the gentleman on the other side perhaps might think that the 200- or 300-year-old cannons up there might have fired. Does that satisfy you as an answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And are you referring, when you say the 200- or 300-year-old cannons, that is the antique cannons which are part of the Old Town fortresses?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So from a point at a greater altitude, they are visible. But of course those cannons haven't fired for the past two or three hundred years.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And how about the walls around the Old Town? Were they ever used to position weapons on or fire out from with either sniper rifles or machine-guns or heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: During the period October to December 1991, was there a presence of international observers in the region?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as I've already said, they were accommodated at the Argentina Hotel and we went to tour the Old Town several times because the Old Town wasn't only shelled on the 6th of December; it was shelled in November as well. So that they would go out to assess the situation every other day. From the hotel looking towards the Old Town, they looked at the Maljutka firings in the Zarkovica area and in the eastern part of the Old Town. So they recorded that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, in the course of your testimony, you referred to JNA attacks carried out in October -- I'm sorry -- on 23rd and 24th of October, 1991. Are those dates correct or could you indicate as to when the October attacks commenced?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the artillery portion or the infantry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I mean the entire JNA attack, whether it be artillery or infantry. I'm referring to October 1991. I'm not referring to December 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the attack and the landing that took place at Dubrovacka, Zupa and Kupari, there was a naval landing on the 23rd and 24th, between the 23rd and 24th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Negodic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. This is a convenient point to -- if -- I'm told -- unless Your Honours wish us to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can break now, but before we do: Mr. Negodic, can you give the Chamber an indication of the total numbers of the defending force that you had in the Dubrovnik area at the 6th of December in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say it might have been 400, 450, outside limit, including the logistics. I can't give you a precise answer, but that is my assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And how many of those were your artillery men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And do I understand from your evidence that most of these had been recruited from the ordinary inhabitants of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And very few of them were in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was the position very different at the beginning of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you give an indication of the size of your defending force then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 250, let's say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Where did the extra numbers come from between the beginning of October and the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were all refugees from the Konavle area, Zupa, and the coastal belt, and they were put up in the hotels and churches and in the basement of the hospital as well. Their entire families were there and they placed themselves at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did reinforcements come in from outside the area between beginning of October and the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, no. No. The Old Town, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wasn't limiting that to the Old Town. I'm speaking of the defending forces in the area of Dubrovnik, that is, the greater Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had in mind the greater Dubrovnik area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we break, in relation to Your Honour's line of questions, may I be permitted just one question before we break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You certainly may, or you can take it up afterwards. I just couldn't contain myself any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: To a question from the Bench, you indicated that the strength of your -- of the Dubrovnik defence was approximately 450 persons. Now, did this include the Dubrovnik -- members of the Dubrovnik police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So in addition to the 450 persons in the region, there were also members of the Dubrovnik police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you be able to give an approximate figure of how many members were there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You would not know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Negodic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's a convenient time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, just before the questions from the Bench, you stated that you remembered the naval landing taking place on 23rd, 24th of October. Up until then, who controlled the seas around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Apparently there's no interpretation, Your Honour. Perhaps ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Negodic, in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question to you. You stated that you remember the naval landing taking place on 23rd, 24th October 1991. Up until then, who controlled the seas around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The seas around Dubrovnik were controlled by the Yugoslav navy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you then indicate what you meant by "the landing" on 23rd, 24th. Landing where?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Dubrovacka, Zupa, Kupari, and the former holiday home or centre there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the course of this particular attack, were your positions fired at by land forces of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day before the landing there was artillery preparation, as we called it. We received knowledge of that in Dubrovacka Rijeka, and at Brgat two and a half thousand different types of shells and mines fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you say the day before that, which date are you indicating; 22nd of October or 23rd October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I'm not quite sure whether it was the 23rd or the 24th. If it was the 23rd, then one day before that. If it was the 24th, then the day before would have been the 23rd, and in my language we refer to that as artillery preparation before combined attack with the landing that is launched.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And could you indicate from which positions, which JNA positions did they fire? To which of the positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It fired at the area, the general area. There was no specific target, just the general area, the area it has to cross en route to the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem with the flow of interpretation, I'm told. I don't know where that is happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think that's probably what my learned friend just indicated to me from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English booth? Can you hear the English channel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to tell you that there was no transcript. What was being said wasn't being recorded on the LiveNote. And that's being going on, Your Honour, now, for several minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't notice this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it's gone wrong with me. I cannot get the English language channel at all. I can't even get my equipment to move off Channel 0 now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I think the transcript is being updated right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've misled us altogether. We thought it had to be Mr. Weiner. I gather we simply must wait a little time. I still cannot change my -- we're getting business now. Yes. Hopefully we will all be able to hear in a language of our choice. Thank you. And transcript is flowing. If you could carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, I'm going to repeat one of those questions again because it's possible that it has not been recorded. Could you indicate as to which JNA positions fired at which Croat positions in the -- during the course of the attack on 23rd, 24th October 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already stated, this was repeated on the old town, the positions of the artillery were not fired at, but the whole region was fired at during this artillery preparation. So the entire area was targeted; Dubrovacka, Zupa, Kupari, Dubac and Brgat, that whole general area, and that was customary. After that, we saw the landing and the takeover of the territory and the shelling, as I have already said, when about two and a half thousand shells and mines fell on the town. Then the landing took place. Our forces withdrew to Brgat and then to Bosanka and then to Srdj and the general Dubrovnik greater area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say so many shells fell on the town, what you mean is the wider area of the Dubrovnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean greater Dubrovnik, that is to say, the broad area around Dubrovnik, and then I gave you the names of the exact positions: Brgat, Bosanka, Dubac, and the broader region around the Dubrovacka-Zupa area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you went on to say your forces withdrew to Brgat and then to Bosanka and then to Srdj. So I take it then during this attack at this particular stage your forces had control over Bosanka and the other two places that you indicated.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under control, but there were no inhabitants or any army, any soldiers, because there was no purpose for them being there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you indicate as to from which JNA positions the fire came? Just a general idea would suffice. Because you indicated the Croat positions to which the fire came into, but I'm now asking what JNA positions fired.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: They opened fire from the Konavle region, with far-reaching artillery pieces, long-range artillery pieces, and from Herzegovina, the mortars and Howitzers were used.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the course of this attack, of course you already indicated and I'm going to ask you again: Was the Old Town shelled?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the beginning. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it shelled at any stage during the course of the attack?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they took over Zarkovica, that's when two mortar mines or shells fell within the walls of the Old Town. Those were the first.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when did they take Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th, roughly. I can't be exact. Because it's been 13 years since then. So even if I were a computer, I couldn't keep track of it all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Negodic [Realtime transcript read in error "Negotic"]. How did you learn of the shelling of the Old Town during this period? Did you observe it or who informed you that the Old Town was shelled during the October attack?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but could you please repeat your question? Before that, may I ask Their Honours to put my surname right. My name is Negodic, with a "D" and not Negotic with a "T." Thank you. N-E-G-O-D-I-C. Thank you. And could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And before we do, just to reassure you, Mr. Negodic, if you notice where that misspelling occurs, there is a little arrow head after it. That is showing that they realise that something has to be corrected there, and they were aware of it before you mentioned it. We know who you are. I hope you're not troubled by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wasn't aware of that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question to you was, Mr. Negodic: How did you learn that the Old Town was shelled during the October attack? Did you observe it yourself or how were you informed of this? As in, were there protests that you're aware of? How did you learn of it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it myself. The command of the town was informed. And it was recorded by the European observers, and the people from the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments. They took note of the exact locations where they fell. That was true for that day and all the other dates afterwards, subsequent to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: During the course of the October attack, were those positions that we looked at on your map, on those two maps, which were in close proximity to the Old Town but outside the Old Town, were those positions active or were they deployed? And I'm referring to the positions at Lazareti.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in October. They weren't active in the month of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How about the position just north of the Old Town, the anti-aircraft weapon? Was that position deployed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I know. It is an anti-aircraft device, and there was no need to resort to it, to use it, because there were no airborne attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the positions at Bogisica Park, was that position deployed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was active for one day in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The position at Gradac Park, was that active?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did your forces respond to the JNA attack?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack was still being launched against Zarkovica at that time. Our forces responded only when the shells started falling on the town. There were just some skirmishes with light machine-guns and the like, rifles, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if -- when your forces did respond, from which positions did they respond, and to which JNA positions? Just a general idea would suffice. We don't have to go into details.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Referring to control of Zarkovica, during the morning, our units remained at Bosanka. Following the shelling of the village of Bosanka, from a number of different directions they withdrew to the fortress of Srdj. If you looked at the map, you could see that the area just underneath Srdj was mined where the road is. One section was not mined, there was no minefield, and in one of the sections and that was left open so that the men could retreat towards the town of Dubrovnik itself through that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Going into the operations in November, do you remember when the November JNA operations commenced?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 3rd of November. The 3rd of November, that's when the operations commenced, and the end came with the cease-fire that was signed on the 8th of November. In the meantime, there were several rounds of talks. A team of negotiators from the town of Dubrovnik, the ECMM, they both went to the Boka military naval sector to negotiate. On behalf of the Boka military naval sector there was Sofronije Jeremic. He made an announcement offering --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. But my question to you is with regard to the time frame of the operations. Do you recall a JNA operation being carried out in the period 8th November to 13th November?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The shelling of the entire area of the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is the attack I'm talking about. When did that attack commence? I mentioned the date 8th November. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 8th of November. The attack -- or rather, the shelling of the general town area lasted from the 3rd until the 8th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just asked you a question as to whether you remember. My question was: Do you recall a JNA operation being carried out in the period 8th November to 13th November? Were there any operations between this period, 8 November to 13th November?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. Perhaps we've been talking at cross-purposes. You are entirely right. It's been so many years. The 8th, the 13th, I'm getting all these dates confused, I'm afraid. You are entirely right, however, and thank you for pointing that out to me. Not from the 3rd to the 8th, but rather from the 8th to the 13th. I apologise, and thank you for setting the record straight there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's all right, Mr. Negodic. Could you just indicate as to when exactly that operation commenced. I'm not asking for the time, but the date. Is the 8th November the correct date?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this is an exaggeration. I believe this is further than anyone should be allowed to go. We have tried to be very patient and we've tried not to intervene, but my learned friend and colleague is obviously leading the witness. We just let it be on one or two occasions, but we think she is now overstepping the mark, and could the Trial Chamber please step in in order to prevent this from continuing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you describe the operation as you remember it. What Croat positions were attacked from which JNA positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, no specific combat positions in the Dubrovnik area were being targeted. Rather, there was continuous targeting of the entire town area; hotels, churches, hospitals, and so on and so forth, including the Old Town itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And who initiated this attack? Was it either of your units or individual members fired to provoke the JNA units, or did your forces initiate the attack, or was it initiated by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack was initiated by the JNA, just like they had started the attack in the area of Konavle, Zupa, Brgat, Zarkovica, and on from there. So that's my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When this attack was going on, at least in the course of this attack at some stage did your forces at this stage have control of Bosanka?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, I'm talking about November. I'm talking about the operations which went on in November. I'm asking you: During this period, did your forces have control of Bosanka?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that on the 23rd, 24th, your forces had control of Bosanka. When did your forces lose control of Bosanka? Would you be able to remember? Was it in the course of this particular attack or a previous attack or subsequent attack?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was just after the 25th of October, because by the 25th of October, we no longer held Bosanka under our control.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the course of the November attack, did your forces respond?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the area of Bosanka, in the Zarkovica area, in the Dubac area, which is the eastern approach to Dubrovnik, and the north-west approach, Sustjepan.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And from which Croat positions was fire sent out from? Where did you fire? Can you identify the Croat positions which were active during this particular operation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16 shells from the Lazareti area to the eastern approach to the Old Town from Dubac, an infantry attack. From the Solitudo camp, camping site, to the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but you said 16 shells from the Lazareti area to the eastern approach to the Old Town from Dubac. Could you be a little bit more specific. It isn't clear as to are you saying that your position at Lazareti fired 16 shells; and if so, to where? Can we clarify that first, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The infantry attack begins in this section of the town, from the direction of Dubac. This is the old approach route that is no longer fit for traffic. This position was used for that purpose. Therefore, the infantry headed that way, taking the old road from Dubac towards the town. 16 shells were fired on those men.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So the infantry you're referring to is the JNA infantry?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And then what other Croat positions fired, and to where?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 120- and 82-millimetre mortars from the combat positions to the north-western approach, the village of Sustjepan, and the slopes of the hill that lies between Bosanka and Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what are the positions, Croat positions fired, or was it only these two, or were there other positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the course of this attack, was the Old Town shelled?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you personally observe this shelling of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could see them firing and there was confirmation from the other side. This was something we couldn't see from our positions at Lapad. So what I have in mind is the eastern section of the town. From there, you can see clearly the places where the shells were landing, especially the ECMM, who were monitoring the trajectories of Maljutka projectiles on the front end of the Old Town and the harbour, where some ships were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you have confirmation later on that the Old Town was in fact shelled during the course of this attack?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received a confirmation in writing that 45 places of worship were either destroyed or damaged, half destroyed. These documents are still in the archive and I believe the ECMM probably still have the recordings and the related documents, because they carried an on-site investigation straight afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: With what weapons was the Old Town shelled? Would you be able to indicate whether they were mortar shelling or artillery, Maljutka, cannons, so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general area of Dubrovnik town was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No -- Old Town. With what weapons was the Old Town shelled? Would you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Old Town, the Old Town was shelled. 82- and 100-millimetre mortars were used. 122-millimetre Howitzers, sporadic tank fire from the Zarkovica area, and continually, the recoilless guns and the Maljutkas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were there any civilian casualties in the course of this attack on the side of the -- on the territory controlled by the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just the wounded. There were civilian casualties in the period between the 8th and 13th November. Again, there were 10 or 11 civilian casualties, and about 80 wounded. Some were seriously wounded and some were lightly wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did your forces suffer any losses?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, in both the two incidents that I referred to, that is, the October attack and the November attack, was there any form of outgoing fire from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you indicated with regard to the November attack that the position at Lazareti was active. Apart from that, were there any positions around Old Town, those positions you identified earlier on as being in close proximity to the Old Town, active during the attack of November?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No other active positions. There was no firing from any of the positions at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What about the anti-aircraft weapons' position just to the north of the Old Town or its alternate position at the Gradac Park? Were those positions deployed or active during the course of the November attack?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said that one day in November, your -- mortar position in Bogisica Park was active. Was it during the course of the attack between the period 8th November to 13th November that Bogisica Park was used by your forces?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't specify the date, but it was in the period between the 8th and 13th. I can't give you the exact date, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And from that position, do you know - and I'm referring to Bogisica Park - which JNA position was targeted?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The positions at Zarkovica and at Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, now, you indicated that the Bogisica Park position was used during the November attack. The anti-aircraft weapon's position which we saw on the map which reflected positions as at 6 December 1991, was that position deployed in November? Was a weapon in that location in November 1991? I'm not asking whether it fired, but was that position there? The weapon, was it there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the course of the attack, the two attacks in October and November, did any units or soldiers belonging to your forces fire, either intentionally or erroneously, at the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the course of the conflict, have you ever experienced a situation where a Croat shell had erroneously impacted on the Old Town? For example, just a hypothetical situation, if I may illustrate: A shell fired from Bogisica to Zarkovica, falling short on the Old Town. Have you ever experienced that type of situation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Old Town was not in the line of firing from the combat position at Bogisica Park. By your leave: The naked eye can monitor the falling of each single shell from that combat position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In November, when the position at Bogisica Park was used, which JNA targets or which JNA positions were targeted from there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, there is no specific firing by the JNA or the paramilitary units on any targets or any positions of the Croatian army in the broader Dubrovnik area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic --

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- my question to you was: From Bogisica Park, which JNA position was targeted on that particular day when the position was active?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I've already said: From the combat position at Bogisica Park, the area between Zarkovica and Bosanka was targeted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what was position between the area between Zarkovica and Bosanka? Were there JNA positions between this area?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between Zarkovica and Bosanka, there is a road that was being used on a daily basis for supplies. JNA weapons were being supplied down that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Negodic, I'm moving on to the incident of the 6th December attack. Do you remember at what time the attack on 6 December commenced? An approximate time would do if you don't remember the exact time.

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be very specific about the time, but it was in the early morning. Daybreak, thereabouts; 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What positions were -- what Croatian positions were attacked first, and from where?

utterances.speaker: IVAN NEGODIC: [Resumed]
